  ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC’S ANALYSIS OF RESIDENTIAL
    RATE IMPACTS FROM THE IMPLEMENTATION OF THE COMMISSION’S
            PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION IN DOCKET No. 58000

       Over the past several months, Oncor conducted an in-depth analysis of the anticipated rate

impact of the changes contained in the Commission’s Proposal for Publication in Docket No.

58000. This analysis endeavored to understand how the commission’s proposed changes would

impact rates for residential ratepayers across the Oncor footprint. The analysis models the

transmission investment and load growth assumptions reflected in the Electric Reliability Council

of Texas’s (“ERCOT”) 2024 Regional Transmission Plan and evaluates two of the Proposed Rules’

principal reforms: (1) the proposed “contractual take-or-pay” transmission cost recovery

framework for customers with demand exceeding 75 MW; and (2) the proposed transition from a

four coincident peak (“4CP”) to a twelve coincident peak (“12CP”) transmission cost allocation

methodology.

       The analysis empirically demonstrates that the changes contained in the proposal for

publication have a net positive effect (reducing rates) for residential customers. In both high and

low load growth scenarios this analysis proves that with implementation of the Docket 58000

changes, large loads are paying not only their full costs to the Texas transmission grid but also

putting negative pressure on residential rates with the additional revenue introduced into the

system through these changes.

  “Oncor recognizes that affordability is a very real concern for Texas families, and policymakers and customers deserve an accurate picture of
  what the investments required to support our state’s growth could mean for their bills,” said Brian Lloyd, Oncor Vice President of
  Regulatory Policy. “Focusing only on the cost of new transmission does not account for the additional customers who will use and pay for
  the new infrastructure. By accounting for the benefits of growth along with the PUCT’s proposed ratemaking reforms, this analysis shows
  how Texas can put downward pressure on residential rates while simultaneously upgrading our grid.”

  What the Analysis Found:

        Even with major new transmission investment, modeled residential transmission costs remain below the 2026 baseline. The analysis
        uses a 2026 baseline of approximately $21.18 per month in transmission costs for an average Oncor residential customer, before
        accounting for the new transmission investment, associated large-load growth and proposed PUCT reforms. When approximately
        $33 billion in investment is modeled with 60 gigawatts (GW) of new large load and the PUCT’s proposed reforms, modeled residential
        transmission costs fall by around $35 per year below the baseline, holding all other factors constant. Over 10 years, that would result
        in an approximately $1.2 billion benefit for Oncor residential customers. A second, lower-growth scenario, pairs approximately $24
        billion in investment with 35 GW of new demand, and modeled residential transmission costs fall by around $15.50 per year below
        the baseline

        New large loads pay for the transmission built to serve them.
        ERCOT’s 2024 RTP identified the transmission needed to serve a system reaching approximately 150 GW of peak demand. While
        serving that growth requires new investment, it also adds customers that help share the cost of that investment as well as the cost of
        current grid. Holding all other factors constant, new large-load customers are actually expected to cover the entirety of the modeled
        2024 RTP costs, under the PUCT’s proposed reforms.

        The PUCT’s proposed reforms would assign a greater share of transmission costs to large loads.
        Texas Senate Bill 6, authored by Senator Phil King, mandates that the PUCT create rules requiring large-load customers to contribute
        directly to the recovery of system interconnection and transmission upgrade costs, thereby protecting residential ratepayers from
        bearing the cost burden. Project No. 58000 proposes changes to how transmission costs are allocated. This includes moving from a
        methodology based on four summer peak periods, known as 4 CP, to peak demand measured across all 12 months, or 12 CP. It also
        proposes a “contractual take-or-pay” framework requiring new large loads above 75 MW to pay transmission costs based on
        contracted capacity once that capacity is available, rather than waiting until it is used. Under the proposed rules, the obligation begins
        when the transmission capacity is available and continues for 20 years. Oncor’s modeling finds that these changes would assign a
        greater share of transmission costs to large-load customers and create substantial downward pressure to residential rates.


  ERCOT developed the 2024 RTP to identify the transmission infrastructure needed to serve approximately 150 GW of peak demand,
  equivalent to the electricity needed to power approximately 37.5 million homes during ERCOT peak demand hours. The approximately $33
  billion plan includes the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP), the 765 kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan (STEP) and numerous other
  69 kV, 138 kV and 345 kV transmission projects and system upgrades. The $33 billion therefore represents the broader 2024 RTP
  investment analyzed by ERCOT, not the cost of 765 kV alone.

  This relationship between investment and new load is increasingly important as Texas experiences rapid growth from oil and gas operations,
  manufacturing, data centers and other large customers seeking to connect to the grid. The investment needed to serve that growth cannot
  be separated from the customers driving the need and helping pay for it. Oncor’s analysis also notes that this shift is already occurring.
  Large commercial and industrial customers paid for approximately 19% of Oncor transmission costs in 2021, rising to 26% in Oncor’s recent
  interim investment filing. Compared with the latest allocation used in Oncor’s last full rate case, the amount assigned to residential
  customers will fall by more than $34 million over the next 12 months.

  It is important to note that this analysis is not a rate forecast. It holds other factors constant to isolate the potential residential impacts of
  the 2024 RTP transmission investment, associated new load and proposed Project No. 58000 ratemaking reforms. It does not account for
  other transmission investment underway or in planning, additional future system needs or other changes that could affect customer bills nor
  does it account for the benefit of upgrading older infrastructure that would be needed anyway. At the same time, the transmission identified
  in the 2024 RTP is also expected to create other benefits for Texas customers through reduced congestion costs and more efficient transfer
  of power across the ERCOT region.

  The full Oncor analysis includes detailed methodology, ratemaking assumptions, scenario modeling, tables and supporting information. Read

 Executive Summary

Texas is experiencing significant growth in electricity demand driven by advanced
manufacturing, oil and gas production, traditional industrial development, data centers, and
broader electrification trends and economic growth.

To support this growth, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) identified
approximately $33 billion of transmission investment in its 2024 Regional Transmission Plan
(RTP), including the Permian Basin Reliability Plan, the 765-kV Strategic Transmission
Expansion Plan (STEP), and other transmission system upgrades needed to maintain reliability
and accommodate future demand of approximately 150 GW. As part of its sensitivity analyses of
the 2024 RTP, ERCOT also evaluated a moderate-growth demand of approximately 125 GW of
peak demand and identified $24 billion of needed transmission investment.

At the outset, it’s important to note that these investment figures do not mean that Texans’ bills
will increase by those amounts: new customers also pay for service, and transmission
investments often significantly reduce congestion costs by unlocking lower-cost generation.
Even so, as Texas evaluates how to fund these investments, a fundamental policy question has
emerged: How do we ensure that customers, especially large loads, pay their fair share of the
transmission-system investment that is needed to serve a growing Texas?
Texas Senate Bill 6 authored by Senator Phil King mandates that the Public Utility Commission
of Texas (PUCT) create rules requiring large-load customers to contribute directly to the
recovery of system interconnection and transmission upgrade costs, thereby protecting
residential ratepayers from bearing the cost burden. In July of 2026, the PUCT issued proposed
rules in Project No. 58000. The two most significant proposed ratemaking reforms include:

   1. The creation of a new “contractual take-or-pay” transmission rate framework for
      customers with demand exceeding 75 MW; under this framework, transmission costs are
      allocated and paid for based on contracted transmission capacity rather than actual peak
      usage. Under the proposed rules, this obligation kicks in when the transmission (rather
      than the customer) is ready, and it applies for two decades, ensuring fair cost allocation
      over time.
   2. The transition from a four coincident peak (4CP) transmission allocation methodology to
      a twelve coincident peak (12CP) methodology, that allocates transmission costs based
      on usage throughout the year rather than during summer peak periods.

To evaluate these proposed reforms, Oncor modeled the approximately $33 billion of
transmission investment identified in ERCOT's 2024 RTP using load growth assumptions
consistent with the RTP.

 The 2024 RTP was developed using a planning assumption of approximately 150 GW of peak
demand. ERCOT’s current peak demand levels are approximately 90 GW. Accordingly, Oncor
evaluated approximately 60 GW (150 GW – 90 GW) of incremental demand growth.

When the PUCT’s changes in docket 58000 are implemented, this analysis yields several main
findings:

   •   Under the scenario that includes approximately 60 GW of new large-load demand,
       residential transmission cost responsibility declines by roughly $35 per year per
       customer.

   •   Under a moderate-growth scenario that includes approximately 35 GW (125 GW – 90
       GW) of new large-load demand, residential transmission cost responsibility declines by
       roughly $15 per year per customer.

   •   The proposed large-load “contractual take-or-pay” customer framework in combination
       with the transition from 4CP to 12CP achieves the goal of ensuring new large loads pay
       for the infrastructure needed to serve them along with creating downward pressure on
       residential rates.

The results indicate that the proposed large-load customer “contractual take-or-pay” framework
and 12CP methodology more closely align transmission cost responsibility with the customers
driving new transmission investment needs. Under both scenarios analyzed, transmission cost
responsibility shifts toward customers creating demand for new infrastructure while reducing
residential customer cost responsibility.

This paper evaluates those proposed reforms under load growth assumptions consistent with
ERCOT's 2024 RTP and examines how they affect transmission cost responsibility among
customer classes.

 I.     Policy Challenge


Historically, transmission costs in ERCOT have been allocated on the basis of usage during the
summer peak periods reflecting the reality that residential air-conditioning load was one of the
primary drivers of transmission needs. Today, a growing share of transmission investment is
being driven by large customers that consume substantial amounts of electricity throughout the
year, including data centers, manufacturing facilities, and other industrial operations. ERCOT's
2024 and 2025 RTPs reflected significant projected growth in electricity demand across the
ERCOT region.

To support this growth, ERCOT's 2024 RTP identified approximately $33 billion of transmission
investment, including the PBRP, the STEP, and other related transmission projects needed to
maintain reliability and accommodate future demand growth.

While the need for new infrastructure has become clear, the size of this transmission build has
required a review of how the cost of those investments should be allocated among customers to
ensure smaller customers are not bearing an inequitable share of the new investment costs.

As a result, policymakers have focused on whether transmission cost allocation methodologies
should evolve to better reflect the customers driving the need for new transmission
infrastructure. Specifically, Senate Bill 6 required the PUCT to review the existing transmission
cost allocation and cost recovery in ERCOT and amend rules as it deemed appropriate. In July
2026, the PUCT proposed new rules in Project No. 58000 to accomplish this goal.

This paper evaluates those proposed reforms and examines how they affect residential
customer transmission cost responsibility under the transmission investment and load growth
assumptions reflected in ERCOT's 2024 RTP.




                                                                                                    4




                                                                                                    9
 II.    How Project No. 58000 Addresses the Challenge

The proposed reforms in Project No. 58000 represent the most significant update to
transmission cost recovery and allocation in ERCOT in more than two decades.

While the rulemaking includes several changes, two provisions are particularly important to
understanding the potential impact on customer bills.

A. Large-Load Customer Tariff Framework

The first major reform creates a new “contractual take-or-pay” transmission cost recovery
framework for very large customers with demands greater than 75 MW.

Under the current transmission rate structure, customers are generally allocated and pay
transmission charges based on their contribution to ERCOT summer peak demand measured
and averaged during the single 15-minute peak intervals in the months of June, July, August,
and September, known as the “4CP methodology.” As a result, large customers that are
significant users of the transmission network who curtail their demand during these intervals
may avoid paying for transmission costs that they cause. Additionally, transmission investment
needed to serve a new large customer may be constructed years before that customer's actual
load fully materializes. During that period, a portion of the cost of the infrastructure may be
borne by existing customers.

Project No. 58000 creates a new framework for large-load customers that requires them to pay
for transmission capacity reserved to serve their demand irrespective of actual consumption, a
“contractual take-or-pay” framework. Under this framework, a load must pay for the level of
service it requested, its contracted for MW level, regardless of actual consumption. This
requires a load to pay for its full impact to the grid. By doing so, the proposal shifts a greater
share of transmission cost responsibility to the customers creating the need for new
infrastructure rather than existing residential, commercial, and smaller industrial customers.

B. Updating Transmission Cost Allocation Through 12CP

The second major reform updates how transmission costs are allocated among customer
classes, by reflecting customers’ peak usage across all twelve months of the year, rather than
just the four hottest months.

As mentioned above, transmission costs have largely been allocated using a 4CP methodology
based on customer demand during peak periods in June, July, August, and September. At the
time the methodology was adopted, residential air-conditioning demand was a primary driver of
transmission planning decisions and the tightest grid conditions with respect to generation
resource adequacy occurred during the same period. The 4CP methodology for many years had

 an added benefit of incentivizing demand response by large customers when the grid was most
constrained with generation.

Texas' load profile has changed significantly since then. Data centers, manufacturing facilities,
industrial operations, and other large customers often operate around the clock and throughout
the year. Additionally, as electrification has occurred across the economy, winter peaks are also
approaching the same level as summer demand. Finally, the changing generation resource mix
in ERCOT has meant that in recent years the periods of most constrained generation availability
has become increasingly divorced from customer peak demand in summer months.

To address this change, the PUCT has proposed transitioning to a 12CP methodology that
reflects peak system usage across all twelve months of the year. The proposed rules also
increase the peak measurement interval from 15 minutes to 30 minutes, reducing opportunities
for customers to temporarily curtail usage solely to avoid transmission charges.

Aligning Cost Responsibility with Transmission Investment Needs

The combination of these two changes reflects today’s reality of transmission planning and
investment drivers. New large-load growth is requiring significant transmission investment to
serve and maintain reliability, and electrification across the economy is resulting in a changing
demand pattern. The following sections evaluate the impact of the proposed Project No. 58000
reforms under the two transmission investment and load growth scenarios identified in the 2024
RTP and examine how they affect residential customer transmission cost responsibility.

 III. Analysis of Project No. 58000 Reforms


To analyze the impact of these two proposed changes, Oncor performed simplified modeling of
ERCOT Transmission Cost of Service (TCOS) and allocation to Oncor customers with the two
2024 RTP scenarios related to incremental load growth and the transmission needed to serve
that growth.

The analysis begins with the 2026 ERCOT-wide transmission revenue requirement of
approximately $6 billion per year. The most recent ERCOT 4CP (2025) of 80,874 MW was used,
of which Oncor comprised 28,677 MW, meaning that Oncor and its customers would be
responsible for 35.46% of overall ERCOT TCOS expense, or around $2.2 billion. Of the 28.7
GW of Oncor 4CP demand in 2025, residential customers comprised 12.2 GW, or 42.4% of
Oncor’s share of ERCOT TCOS. This results in around $910 million of annual transmission
expense allocated to residential customers on Oncor’s system, with the typical residential
customer paying around $21 per month. This residential allocation is the baseline for the
subsequent analyses.

 SCENARIO 1: $33 billion new transmission investment, 60 GW new large
load, 12CP Allocation

The modeling used the $33 billion of transmission investment identified in ERCOT's 2024 RTP
and assumed 60 GW of incremental demand growth modeled under the proposed large-load

impact of the proposed Project No. 58000 reforms under load growth assumptions generally
consistent with those evaluated in the 2024 RTP.

 To be conservative:

      •     In order to isolate the impacts of the PUCT's proposed rule changes, no growth in
            residential or other customer classes was assumed even though additional customer
            growth would provide more demand over which to spread transmission costs and could
            further reduce cost responsibility on a per-customer basis.3

      •     Total load is restrained to 150 GW of peak demand to align with the 2024 RTP in order

The incremental 60 GW of large load demand is treated as its own new rate class that will be
allocated transmission costs in accordance with a full 60 GW of demand. This is consistent with
the PUCT’s proposed rule changes as discussed above. For purposes of this analysis, all of the
load is reflected as incremental load to Oncor for both the allocation of transmission costs to
Oncor and the allocation across retail customer classes, instead of allocated across ERCOT
utilities.

This is because under the PUCT’s proposed rule changes, the allocation of transmission costs
for large loads “follows” the load through the allocation to the utility and then among retail
customers. This simplification has no material effect on the outcome to Oncor customers.

Finally, the analysis calculates the impact of the second change in the PUCT’s proposed rules
related to the change to a 12CP methodology.6 Oncor’s residential customers share of Oncor’s
TCOS under a 12CP methodology would fall to 39.1% from the current 42.4% allocation under
the 4CP methodology.7

 The results of this analysis are as follows and shown below in Table 3.

     •     Overall annual ERCOT TCOS revenue requirement rises by $3.83 billion to $9.88 billion.

     •     Total new ERCOT 4CP is 141 GW, representing the addition of the 60 GW of
           incremental large load from the 2026 ERCOT 4CP.

     •     Because all of the large load is assumed to be “Oncor load,” Oncor’s share of ERCOT-
           wide TCOS rises to 62.95%, or $6.22 billion.

     •     The residential allocation of costs falls to 13.7% of Oncor’s TCOS share and total TCOS
           allocated to the residential class falls by $57 million, or approximately $1.32 per month
           per residential customer.8

     •     The impact of the change from 4CP allocation among Oncor’s customer classes to 12CP
           results in an additional shift of costs away from the residential class of $67 million, or
           approximately $1.56 per month per residential customer.

     •     The total modeled residential reduction from the baseline is $2.89 per customer per
           month, or approximately $34.65 per year.


The analysis indicates that the PUCT’s proposed ratemaking reforms achieve the twin goals of
ensuring new large load pays for the infrastructure build out needed to serve them, as well as
reducing residential rates, even before accounting for other benefits of the 2024 RTP such as
reduced congestion and modernization of aged infrastructure.

 IV. Conclusion

The proposed Project No. 58000 reforms achieve the objective of better aligning transmission
cost responsibility with the customers driving the need for new transmission investment.

Under both scenarios evaluated, the proposed large-load customer “contractual take-or-pay”
framework shifts a meaningful portion of the transmission cost burden to the customers driving
new transmission investment needs. At the same time, the proposed transition from a 4CP
methodology to a 12CP methodology better aligns transmission cost allocation with year-round
use of the transmission system.

When these reforms are applied to the transmission investments identified in ERCOT's 2024
RTP, residential customer transmission cost responsibility declines under both scenarios
analyzed. Under the scenario reflecting approximately $33 billion of transmission investment
and 60 GW of incremental demand growth, residential transmission cost responsibility declines
by approximately $35 per year. Under the lower-growth scenario reflecting approximately $24
billion of transmission investment and 35 GW of incremental demand growth, residential
transmission cost responsibility declines by approximately $15 per year.

While these results are based on a study of the 2024 RTP values, they are indicative of the
results that would be expected under other scenarios with the implementation of Project 58000’s
proposed changes.

While future customer rates will ultimately depend on many factors beyond the scope of this
analysis, including future transmission investments, load growth, regulatory decisions, and
market conditions, the results demonstrate that the proposed Project No. 58000 reforms
materially affect how transmission costs are allocated among customer classes to the benefit of
the residential ratepayer.

More broadly, the analysis demonstrates that the combination of a large-load customer
“contractual take-or-pay” framework and a 12CP allocation methodology better aligns
transmission cost responsibility with the customers creating the need for new transmission
infrastructure. As Texas continues to experience significant economic and load growth, these
reforms support the broader objective of ensuring that growth contributes to the infrastructure
required to serve it while reducing residential customer transmission cost responsibility.

Ultimately, the proposed reforms provide a framework for accommodating continued economic
growth while more closely aligning transmission cost responsibility with transmission investment
needs, benefiting both the long-term development of the Texas electric system and the
customers who rely upon it.

Utility Ratemaking and Transmission Cost Allocation

Electric utilities operate under a highly regulated regime where prices cannot be adjusted
without the approval of a regulator.

While there are a variety of methods used to set rates, Texas utilizes a retrospective (historical)
cost method where rates are based on a historical set of costs with full costs examined
generally every four years during a rate case. In between full rate cases, utilities can update
rates to reflect incremental investment. At a high level, electric utility rates are comprised of the
following cost elements:

   •   Return of investment through depreciation of assets over their expected life;
   •   Return on investment to compensate debt and equity holders for the funds
       borrowed/utilized to build the assets;
   •   Operations and maintenance expense; and
   •   Taxes (federal, state and local, and franchise fees).

When it comes to recovery of transmission investment in the ERCOT market, transmission
costs are spread among all customers in the ERCOT region, irrespective of which utility builds
the assets.

Within a rate proceeding, a detailed listing of utility costs is laid out in a system of line-item
accounts prescribed by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). Each of these line
items is allocated to customer classes based on the underlying driver of the cost. For example,
the cost of meters may be allocated among customer classes based on the number and type of
meters used to serve each class, while street lighting costs are directly assigned to the street
lighting class. This process is repeated across hundreds of accounts to develop the overall
allocation of costs among customer classes.

When it comes to capital investment, allocation to customer classes is done on the basis of
what drives the investment need, and transmission and distribution have different drivers. For
distribution poles and wires, utilities generally size and build distribution lines to meet the
simultaneous demand that all customers may put on the line so that at the hottest (or coldest)
period of the year, the facility is adequate to serve the maximum use of every customer at the
same time.

In contrast, transmission investment is driven more by the need to adequately serve the
aggregate peak of all customers – recognizing that not all customers across the entirety of the
ERCOT grid will be simultaneously using their peak demand. In 2000, the PUCT concluded that
the main driver of transmission investment was the need to meet the summer peak demand in

 June, July, August, and September, when residential air conditioning and other weather-
sensitive demand would peak.

In recognition that transmission cost allocation policy had not been reviewed in the decades
since this prior determination, SB 6 required the PUCT to re-examine the drivers of transmission
investment and determine if a change to cost allocation is warranted. The changes proposed by
the PUCT are described in this paper, but it is important to note that growth in large customers
has already led to a shift of overall transmission costs away from smaller customers, namely
residential customers.

In Oncor’s rate proceeding in 2022, which utilized data from 2021, large commercial and
industrial customers were responsible for approximately 19% of transmission costs. In Oncor’s
next full rate proceeding in 2025, using 2024 data, large commercial and industrial customers
were responsible for 25% of transmission costs – even using the 4CP methodology. Prior to the
2025 Legislative Session, updates to these allocation factors only occurred in these full rate
proceedings, meaning that in this emerging era of larger customer load growth, smaller
customers would end up subsidizing these customers between rate cases, with residential and
small commercial rates higher than they should have been.

With the consolidation of interim rate proceedings into a single annual proceeding through HB
5247 for certain utilities, these cost allocation updates will now occur annually, better aligning
the allocation of growing transmission investment with the customers driving the need for that
investment. In Oncor's recent interim investment filing, large commercial and industrial
customers were allocated approximately 26% of transmission costs, resulting in an estimated
benefit of more than $30 million to residential customers compared to the allocation used in
Oncor's last full rate case.

 I.     Policy Challenge


Historically, transmission costs in ERCOT have been allocated on the basis of usage during the
summer peak periods reflecting the reality that residential air-conditioning load was one of the
primary drivers of transmission needs. Today, a growing share of transmission investment is
being driven by large customers that consume substantial amounts of electricity throughout the
year, including data centers, manufacturing facilities, and other industrial operations. ERCOT's
2024 and 2025 RTPs reflected significant projected growth in electricity demand across the
ERCOT region.

To support this growth, ERCOT's 2024 RTP identified approximately $33 billion of transmission
investment, including the PBRP, the STEP, and other related transmission projects needed to
maintain reliability and accommodate future demand growth.

While the need for new infrastructure has become clear, the size of this transmission build has
required a review of how the cost of those investments should be allocated among customers to
ensure smaller customers are not bearing an inequitable share of the new investment costs.

As a result, policymakers have focused on whether transmission cost allocation methodologies
should evolve to better reflect the customers driving the need for new transmission
infrastructure. Specifically, Senate Bill 6 required the PUCT to review the existing transmission
cost allocation and cost recovery in ERCOT and amend rules as it deemed appropriate. In July
2026, the PUCT proposed new rules in Project No. 58000 to accomplish this goal.

This paper evaluates those proposed reforms and examines how they affect residential
customer transmission cost responsibility under the transmission investment and load growth
assumptions reflected in ERCOT's 2024 RTR

 Il.     How Project No. 58000 Addresses the Challenge

The proposed reforms in Project No. 58000 represent the most significant update to
transmission cost recovery and allocation in ERCOT in more than two decades.

While the rulemaking includes several changes, two provisions are particularly important to
understanding the potential impact on customer bills.

A. Large-Load Customer Tariff Framework

The first major reform creates a new "contractual take-or-pay" transmission cost recovery
framework for very large customers with demands greater than 75 MW.

Under the current transmission rate structure, customers are generally allocated and pay
transmission charges based on their contribution to ERCOT summer peak demand measured
and averaged during the single 15-minute peak intervals in the months of June, July, August,
and September, known as the "4CP methodology." As a result, large customers that are
significant users of the transmission network who curtail their demand during these intervals
may avoid paying for transmission costs that they cause. Additionally, transmission investment
needed to serve a new large customer may be constructed years before that customer's actual
load fully materializes. During that period, a portion of the cost of the infrastructure may be
borne by existing customers.

Project No. 58000 creates a new framework for large-load customers that requires them to pay
for transmission capacity reserved to serve their demand irrespective of actual consumption, a
"contractual take-or-pay" framework. Under this framework, a load must pay for the level of
service it requested, its contracted for MW level, regardless of actual consumption. This
requires a load to pay for its full impact to the grid. By doing so, the proposal shifts a greater
share of transmission cost responsibility to the customers creating the need for new
infrastructure rather than existing residential, commercial, and smaller industrial customers.

B. Updating Transmission Cost Allocation Through 12CP

The second major reform updates how transmission costs are allocated among customer
classes, by reflecting customers' peak usage across all twelve months of the year, rather than
just the four hottest months.

As mentioned above, transmission costs have largely been allocated using a 4CP methodology
based on customer demand during peak periods in June, July, August, and September. At the
time the methodology was adopted, residential air-conditioning demand was a primary driver of
transmission planning decisions and the tightest grid conditions with respect to generation
resource adequacy occurred during the same period. The 4CP methodology for many years had

Texas' load profile has changed significantly since then. Data centers, manufacturing facilities,
industrial operations, and other large customers often operate around the clock and throughout
the year. Additionally, as electrification has occurred across the economy, winter peaks are also
approaching the same level as summer demand. Finally, the changing generation resource mix
in ERCOT has meant that in recent years the periods of most constrained generation availability
has become increasingly divorced from customer peak demand in summer months.

To address this change, the PUCT has proposed transitioning to a 12CP methodology that
reflects peak system usage across all twelve months of the year. The proposed rules also
increase the peak measurement interval from 15 minutes to 30 minutes, reducing opportunities
for customers to temporarily curtail usage solely to avoid transmission charges.

investment drivers. New large-load growth is requiring significant transmission investment to
serve and maintain reliability, and electrification across the economy is resulting in a changing
demand pattern. The following sections evaluate the impact of the proposed Project No. 58000
reforms under the two transmission investment and load growth scenarios identified in the 2024
RTP and examine how they affect residential customer transmission cost responsibility.

 IV. Conclusion

The proposed Project No. 58000 reforms achieve the objective of better aligning transmission
cost responsibility with the customers driving the need for new transmission investment.

Under both scenarios evaluated, the proposed large-load customer "contractual take-or-pay"
framework shifts a meaningful portion of the transmission cost burden to the customers driving
new transmission investment needs. At the same time, the proposed transition from a 4CP
methodology to a 12CP methodology better aligns transmission cost allocation with year-round
use of the transmission system.

When these reforms are applied to the transmission investments identified in ERCOT's 2024
RTP, residential customer transmission cost responsibility declines under both scenarios
analyzed. Under the scenario reflecting approximately $33 billion of transmission investment
and 60 GW of incremental demand growth, residential transmission cost responsibility declines
by approximately $35 per year. Under the lower-growth scenario reflecting approximately $24
billion of transmission investment and 35 GW of incremental demand growth, residential
transmission cost responsibility declines by approximately $15 per year.

While these results are based on a study of the 2024 RTP values, they are indicative of the
results that would be expected under other scenarios with the implementation of Project 58000's
proposed changes.
While future customer rates will ultimately depend on many factors beyond the scope of this
analysis, including future transmission investments, load growth, regulatory decisions, and
market conditions, the results demonstrate that the proposed Project No. 58000 reforms
materially affect how transmission costs are allocated among customer classes to the benefit of
the residential ratepayer.

More broadly, the analysis demonstrates that the combination of a large-load customer
"contractual take-or-pay" framework and a 12CP allocation methodology better aligns
transmission cost responsibility with the customers creating the need for new transmission
infrastructure. As Texas continues to experience significant economic and load growth, these
reforms support the broader objective of ensuring that growth contributes to the infrastructure
required to serve it while reducing residential customer transmission cost responsibility.

Ultimately, the proposed reforms provide a framework for accommodating continued economic
growth while more closely aligning transmission cost responsibility with transmission investment
needs, benefiting both the long-term development of the Texas electric system and the
customers who rely upon it.

Utility Ratemaking and Transmission Cost Allocation

Electric utilities operate under a highly regulated regime where prices cannot be adjusted
without the approval of a regulator.

While there are a variety of methods used to set rates, Texas utilizes a retrospective (historical)
cost method where rates are based on a historical set of costs with full costs examined
generally every four years during a rate case. In between full rate cases, utilities can update
rates to reflect incremental investment. At a high level, electric utility rates are comprised of the
following cost elements:

    •   Return of investment through depreciation of assets over their expected life;
    •   Return on investment to compensate debt and equity holders for the funds
        borrowed/utilized to build the assets;
    •   Operations and maintenance expense; and
    •   Taxes (federal, state and local, and franchise fees).

When it comes to recovery of transmission investment in the ERCOT market, transmission
costs are spread among all customers in the ERCOT region, irrespective of which utility builds
the assets.

Within a rate proceeding, a detailed listing of utility costs is laid out in a system of line-item
accounts prescribed by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). Each of these line
items is allocated to customer classes based on the underlying driver of the cost. For example,
the cost of meters may be allocated among customer classes based on the number and type of
meters used to serve each class, while street lighting costs are directly assigned to the street
lighting class. This process is repeated across hundreds of accounts to develop the overall
allocation of costs among customer classes.

When it comes to capital investment, allocation to customer classes is done on the basis of
what drives the investment need, and transmission and distribution have different drivers. For
distribution poles and wires, utilities generally size and build distribution lines to meet the
simultaneous demand that all customers may put on the line so that at the hottest (or coldest)
period of the year, the facility is adequate to serve the maximum use of every customer at the
same time.

In contrast, transmission investment is driven more by the need to adequately serve the
aggregate peak of all customers - recognizing that not all customers across the entirety of the
ERCOT grid will be simultaneously using their peak demand. In 2000, the PUCT concluded that
the main driver of transmission investment was the need to meet the summer peak demand in

sensitive demand would peak.

In recognition that transmission cost allocation policy had not been reviewed in the decades
since this prior determination, SB 6 required the PUCT to re-examine the drivers of transmission
investment and determine if a change to cost allocation is warranted. The changes proposed by
the PUCT are described in this paper, but it is important to note that growth in large customers
has already led to a shift of overall transmission costs away from smaller customers, namely
residential customers.

In Oncor's rate proceeding in 2022, which utilized data from 2021, large commercial and
industrial customers were responsible for approximately 19% of transmission costs. In Oncor's
next full rate proceeding in 2025, using 2024 data, large commercial and industrial customers
were responsible for 25% of transmission costs - even using the 4CP methodology. Prior to the
2025 Legislative Session, updates to these allocation factors only occurred in these full rate
proceedings, meaning that in this emerging era of larger customer load growth, smaller
customers would end up subsidizing these customers between rate cases, with residential and
small commercial rates higher than they should have been.

With the consolidation of interim rate proceedings into a single annual proceeding through HB
5247 for certain utilities, these cost allocation updates will now occur annually, better aligning
the allocation of growing transmission investment with the customers driving the need for that
investment. In Oncor's recent interim investment filing, large commercial and industrial
customers were allocated approximately 26% of transmission costs, resulting in an estimated
benefit of more than $30 million to residential customers compared to the allocation used in
Oncor's last full rate case.
